sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Mycena pura (Pers.) P. Kumm., the Lilac Mycena, is a small species with a 2–5 cm cap (occasionally to 6.5 cm), initially convex or shallowly conical, then spreading, sometimes with a low blunt umbo or a central depression. The cap is hygrophanous and translucently striate when wet; its color varies widely from lilac, pink and violet to grey, and it may fade or become whitish. The whitish to pink-lilac gills are attached to the stem, sometimes sinuate or with a short decurrent tooth; they are moderately close to rather distant and may become interveined with age. A three-gene phylogeny resolved 11 concordant phylogenetic species in the M. pura complex, most of them cryptic; these phylogenetic units are not automatically formally named species and cannot always be distinguished by macroscopic morphology alone.

sections.title: Stem, flesh and habitat
sections.text: The hollow stem is about 4–9 cm by 2–7 mm; it is fragile, whitish to lilac or cap-colored, often paler near the top, with whitish fibrils at the base. The flesh is thin, soft and pale, with a characteristic radish-like odor. This saprotroph grows in humus, leaf litter and needle litter, especially in deciduous or coniferous woodland. Northern European sources report it mainly in summer and autumn, with fruiting season varying by region.

sections.title: Toxicity and caution
sections.text: The DGfM and the Norwegian Poison Information Centre classify M. pura among species associated with muscarinic poisoning. A 1976 chemical study detected low concentrations of muscarine stereoisomers in fruit bodies (up to 2 mg/100 g dry weight); however, the French Society of Emergency Medicine notes that the presence of pharmacologically active muscarine and the species-specific clinical role of M. pura are debated. These sources do not support assigning this species a precise onset time or symptom profile. Anses reports confusions involving Mycena during searches for Laccaria, including one report identified as M. rosea; this alone does not prove a particular toxic mechanism in M. pura. Do not eat it; contact a poison centre if ingested.

traits: Hygrophanous cap, translucently striate when wet, highly variable from lilac/pink/violet to grey or whitish; often with a blunt low umbo
Whitish to pink or lilac gills, attached to the stem, moderately close to rather distant, sometimes becoming interveined; spore print white
Hollow, pale to lilac stem, often with white basal fibrils; thin flesh with radish-like odor
Saprotroph of woodland litter; difficult to identify from a single image because colors vary widely
safetyNote: Do not eat. Toxicology references often classify this species as muscarinic, but the clinical significance and role of active muscarine in M. pura are debated. No species-specific onset time or symptom profile is asserted here. Contact a poison centre after ingestion.
